title: A Midterm Setback Complicates Rubio's Latin America Policy
gist: Orlando J. Pérez argues the Nov. 3, 2026 US midterms - near-losses for Miami-Dade Republicans Díaz-Balart and Salazar and Democratic control of the Senate and House Foreign Affairs Committee from January - raise the political cost of Rubio's Latin America policy: pressure for a Venezuelan election date and Machado's inclusion, likely congressional conditions on the Venezuela oil deal, and oversight of the Cuba escalation and Shield of the Americas security aid. He flags the eight-week lame-duck window as the 'cheapest moment' for a quick Cuba move.

themes.theme: Miami-Dade near-losses as a warning to Rubio

insights.claim: In the Nov. 3, 2026 US midterms, Miami-Dade Republicans who carry the administration's Venezuela/Cuba policy nearly lost: Mario Díaz-Balart finished less than a point ahead of Democrat Nicole Locklin and María Elvira Salazar led by about 1,000 votes heading toward a recount.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Erosion of Rubio's home political base weakens domestic cover for hardline Venezuela/Cuba policy; watch the Salazar recount.
insights.quote: Mario Díaz-Balart finished less than a point ahead of Democrat Nicole Locklin

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has effectively run US policy toward Latin America since the start of Trump's second term, building his Venezuela and Cuba positions on Miami-Dade constituency support.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Rubio's personal political incentives are a key driver of US hemispheric policy, so his domestic standing matters for sanctions/oil outcomes.
insights.quote: For all practical purposes, since the start of Donald Trump’s second term, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has run Washington’s policy toward Latin America.
insights.locator: For all practical purposes, since the start

insights.claim: Trump still holds major tools (oil licenses, sanctions, recognition, the military) and nothing in the midterm results forces him to use them differently, but the election raised the price of using them without explanation to Congress and Miami-Dade voters.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Expect policy continuity but more congressional friction and justification requirements rather than a reversal.
insights.quote: the election raised the price of using them without explanation in Congress

themes.theme: Venezuela: election calendar and Machado's exclusion

insights.claim: Rubio has accepted acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez as a partner, built oil concessions around her government, and kept opposition leader María Corina Machado out of the negotiating room.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: US oil-concession access in Venezuela is tied to a Rodríguez-government partnership whose legitimacy is politically contested in Washington.

insights.claim: Washington's Venezuela roadmap calls for a new Supreme Court by year-end 2026 and a new electoral council after, but Rodríguez's declaration of presidential vacancy - the legal step starting the constitutional clock toward a vote - still has no date.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: The missing vacancy declaration is the key milestone to watch for whether a Venezuelan election actually materializes.
insights.quote: Rodríguez’s declaration of presidential vacancy—the necessary legal step that will start the constitutional clock toward a vote—still has no date
insights.locator: The first pressure point is the calendar.

insights.claim: On Nov. 5, Rubio told The New York Times that Venezuelan elections would 'ideally' take place next year, while declining to guarantee them before Trump leaves office in January 2029.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Absence of a firm commitment leaves Venezuelan political transition timing - and oil-license durability - open-ended.
insights.quote: elections would “ideally” take place next year

insights.claim: Florida Republicans who nearly lost have incentive to demand a Venezuelan election date, and Machado - who returned to Venezuela Oct. 25, endorsed Rubio's sequence and called for elections next year - gives them a way to do so without breaking with the White House.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Watch for Florida GOP pressure to include Machado in the formal dialogue led by Dinorah Figuera and Jorge Rodríguez; inclusion would signal a firmer transition path.
insights.quote: She is the obvious bridge back to Venezuelan voters

insights.claim: Trump's Sept. 22 UN address describing Venezuela policy as 'to the victor belong the spoils', and his meeting with Rodríguez the same day authorities reportedly blocked a Machado return attempt, made the partnership harder to defend at home.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Framing of Venezuela as a resource prize amplifies the political vulnerability of the oil deal.

themes.theme: Congressional leverage over the Venezuela oil deal

insights.claim: From January, Democrats will control the Senate and run the House Foreign Affairs Committee, after Republicans on the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee voted down a Democratic attempt in September to subpoena records on the Venezuela oil deal.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Expect subpoenas and oversight hearings on the Venezuela oil arrangement in 2027.
insights.locator: The oil deal faces a different

insights.claim: Democrats could write conditions into must-pass bills tying new Venezuelan oil licenses to dated electoral steps, as Congress did in 2016 when it tied Central American aid to anti-corruption certifications; accepting such conditions may become the administration's cheapest way to protect the deal.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Energy companies holding or seeking Venezuelan licenses face rising risk of conditionality tied to election milestones.
insights.quote: Accepting new conditions may become the administration’s cheapest way to protect it.

insights.claim: Machado has said the Venezuela oil deal lacks 'the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,' and Salazar wrote in a since-deleted post that it 'has an expiration date.'
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Even allies of the administration signal the oil deal is not politically durable - a tail risk for contract longevity.

themes.theme: Cuba: escalation vs. a private-sector relief strategy

insights.claim: The administration escalated on Cuba in October: on Oct. 23 Trump said warships returning from the Iran war would 'pass Cuba,' and Rubio urged Cubans on X to 'seize this opportunity' through 'a discrete partnership with the CIA.'
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Elevated risk of US-Cuba military/political crisis; a regional geopolitical tail risk to monitor.

insights.claim: An FIU poll found 74% of respondents backed US assistance to Cuba's private sector for humanitarian relief, a majority even among Republicans; the author argues pairing sanctions on the Cuban state with support for private businesses would satisfy Cuban Americans' dual desire for regime pressure and family relief.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: A pivot to private-sector support in Cuba would open limited commercial channels; watch for policy signals in that direction.
insights.quote: 74% of respondents backed U.S. assistance to Cuba’s private sector for humanitarian relief

insights.claim: The same FIU polling shows 73% of Miami-Dade Cuban Americans support US military action to overthrow the Cuban government, versus only 17% of Americans nationally favoring force to take the island in an August Economist/YouGov poll.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: The gap between Miami's and national opinion means a Cuba military move would be locally popular but nationally risky.
insights.quote: only 17% of Americans favored using force to take control of the island

insights.claim: Further Cuba escalation would risk a crisis just as Congress gains the power to investigate how it started.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Escalation in Cuba now carries greater oversight and political-blowback risk for the administration.
insights.quote: risking a crisis just as Congress gains the power to ask how it started

themes.theme: Rubio's 2028 calculus and the lame-duck window

insights.claim: A secretary of state with presidential ambitions has every incentive to seek a quick result in Cuba before a campaign begins, and the eight weeks before the new Congress takes office, with Republicans still controlling both chambers, are the cheapest moment to try.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Raise watch for Cuba-related US action in the Nov. 2026-Jan. 2027 lame-duck window.
insights.quote: the eight weeks before the new Congress takes office, with Republicans still in control of both chambers, are the cheapest moment to try
insights.locator: A secretary of state with presidential

insights.claim: Trump said Oct. 30 the Cuban government would not last much longer and that Rubio was watching closely, tying Rubio's record to an outcome he does not control; Rubio says serving through the end of Trump's term has 'always been my plan.'
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Rubio's career incentives are linked to Cuban regime change, raising the odds of continued pressure.

insights.claim: Rubio and JD Vance are on opposite sides of the Iran war: Vance blamed it for the Republican midterm losses while on Nov. 5 Rubio defended it as 'the price of leadership,' though Rubio has said he would back Vance in 2028.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: An emerging intra-GOP split over the Iran war shapes 2028 succession and foreign-policy direction.

themes.theme: Shield of the Americas exposed to a Democratic House

insights.claim: The Shield of the Americas security coalition, launched by Trump in March with right-leaning governments, expanded to 15 members by September; Argentina, Ecuador, El Salvador, Colombia and Peru have tied their security strategies to Trump's personal approval.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Governments heavily aligned with Trump face reduced US policy certainty as Congress shifts.

insights.claim: A Democratic House writes the appropriations for Shield of the Americas allies' security assistance and can attach human rights vetting and limits on the use of force, so allies who bet on the White House must now also answer to Congress.
insights.speaker: ORLANDO J. PÉREZ
insights.so_what: Expect conditionality on US security aid to aligned Latin American governments, a modest negative for their security agendas.
insights.quote: Allies who bet on the White House must now also answer to a Washington that moved to the left on Nov. 3
